newsitem.title: INDIA: New India debt norms welcomed, but problems remain.
newsitem.headline: New India debt norms welcomed, but problems remain.

text.p: Analysts on Monday welcomed the relaxation of norms for foreign investment in Indian debt but said they did not expect any immediate impact in the market.

India's capital market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) released guidelines on Saturday, giving foreign institutional investors (FIIs) greater freedom to invest in Indian debt.
"It is a positive development but I do not think there will be any major impact in the short term," said banking analyst Tabassum Inamdar at Jardine Fleming Broking India.
"The relaxations of norms is welcome but FII inflows will be constrained by the fact that there are no hedging instruments available to tackle long-term currency exposures."
She said it would be difficult for investors to take a long- term view, given these constraints.
Other analysts agreed saying the move, while welcome, was unlikely to result in an FII stampede to set up debt funds.
"This is a move in the right direction," said Sanjeev Mohta, head of research at James Capel B&K.
"It is an indication that the government realises the importance of the debt market. But without an active secondary market it's difficult to see any immediate impact."
There is practically no secondary market for India debt. Even government securities, the most liquid of investments the world over, suffer from illiquidity.
The daily average trades in October on the wholesale debt segment on the National Stock Exchange was around two billion rupees against outstanding stock of over 1,761 billion rupees, analysts said.
Corporate debt is hardly traded in India and there is no reliable data on either issues of such securities or trades.
